summary: Jon Postel's account of the ad hoc Telnet protocol as it was then understood, including the Network Virtual Terminal, with proposed changes. He states plainly that there was no Official Telnet Protocol yet. It was updated by RFC 435.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes an early version of Telnet, a way to use a remote computer through a terminal connection. It defines shared character and control conventions, while openly noting that the protocol was still evolving.

how did early telnet represent line endings
subtitle: A 1972 account of the evolving Telnet protocol and its network virtual terminal.

tldr.problem: Users needed a common way to connect terminals at one site to processes on another host, despite differences in local terminal and operating-system behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a Network Virtual Terminal using 8-bit character codes, a shared CR-LF line ending, and Telnet control signals embedded in a character stream.
tldr.outcome: The author calls the protocol ad hoc, says there is no official Telnet protocol, and proposes changes for discussion. Unit metadata lists RFC 435 as an update.

today: RFC 318 is an early Telnet description, and the unit metadata lists RFC 435 as an update to it.

sections.title: An Evolving Protocol
sections.content:
The author presents his understanding of an informal Telnet protocol, not a settled official specification. The memo gathers existing conventions, describes how they work, and proposes changes for discussion.

Telnet's goal is to connect terminal devices at one site to processes at another site without requiring each host to know the other host's local terminal details.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a description of a protocol that was still being worked out. It explains shared rules for remote terminal sessions and invites discussion of proposed changes.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal
sections.content:
The Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) is a two-way character device with a keyboard and printer. Character codes are 8 bits wide; codes 0 through 127 are US-ASCII, while the memo reserves codes 128 through 255 for special control signals.

The common end-of-line sequence is carriage return followed by line feed. A sending site and receiving site translate that shared representation to their local terminal behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVT gives different computers a shared way to represent keyboard input and screen output. Each site translates those characters to match its own equipment.

sections.title: Data and Control Signals
sections.content:
Telnet carries a character stream with control signals embedded in it. The memo describes signals for break, no operation, echo, suppressing echo, hiding input, and synchronizing after urgent input.

For synchronization, a DATA MARK in the stream works with an interrupt signal from the host-to-host protocol. The NVT conventions also define ASCII as the ordinary character set and describe how control signals can be used during a session.
sections.plainLanguage: Alongside ordinary characters, Telnet carries signals that control the session. These can request actions such as echoing characters or marking a point for synchronization.

sections.title: Implementation and Proposed Changes
sections.content:
The memo describes standard and minimum implementations for using and serving hosts. Both sides need to support the shared line-ending convention, while their responsibilities for local echo and control signals differ.

In a later section, the author proposes deleting several signals and changing minimum implementation rules. These are proposals for discussion, not a claim that those changes had become settled protocol requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts need compatible ways to translate characters and handle the session's control signals. The memo also suggests changes, but presents them as proposals rather than final rules.
